utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since this is at least my first appearance in the case against you, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to introduce myself. I'm Judge Orie. May I have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mark Harmon. To my right is Mr. Alan Tieger. We represent the Office of the Prosecutor in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. May I have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Doesn't work, Your Honour. Your Honour, Deyan Brashich. I'm lead counsel for the defendant. And with me is Mr. Nikola Kostich. Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brashich. Good afternoon too, of course, to everyone. Yes. I take it that you prefer to have a microphone that functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I think I'll be doing most of the speaking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is, I take it, the last Status Conference that will take place before the commencement of the trial. The commencement of the trial has been scheduled for the 12th of May of this year. The Trial Chamber will, as you might know by now, will be composed of myself as Presiding Judge, by Judge El Mahdi, and a new ad litem Judge that has to be appointed and, of course, assigned to this case. Once this has been done, I believe it will be appropriate for call for a second Pre-Trial Conference with the attendance of the new ad litem Judge. That could take place shortly before the beginning of the trial. The parties, of course, will be notified in due course of the date for such a new Pre-Trial Conference. The purpose of this Status Conference of today is to settle a few -- small number of issues that are related to the completion of the pre-trial stage of this case and also for the preparation of the trial itself. Therefore, I would like to first discuss with you very briefly the agenda. I take it you have received a provisional agenda from Mr. Harhoff, is that correct, on which appears outstanding motions, the submission of lists of viva voce witnesses and 92 bis statements and transcripts and submission of the list of exhibits. The third issue, depositions under Rule 71 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Number four, the estimated length of the Prosecution's case. Rules of the road, a question mark is put behind a trial management seminar. Further is on the agenda the health and the condition of you, Mr. Krajisnik, the accused, and any other matters raised by the parties. Is there anything at this very moment you'd like to add to the agenda or would there be any observation you'd like to make in view of the agenda suggested?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's nothing on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Nothing on behalf of the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we'll proceed with the agenda. The first item to be the outstanding motions. As far as I am aware of, but I still have to grow into the case as well, there are six outstanding motions as far as I'm aware of. The first one is a Defence motion of the 13th of September, 2002. That's the motion applying for an order suppressing illegally intercepted communications. I would call that a first category on its own. Then we have four motions pending on the disclosure of exculpatory material, one of the 29th of December, 2002, that would concern exculpatory material that has been obtained or gathered in what then was the case against Mr. Raznjatovic. The next one is a motion of the 9th of January, 2003, exculpatory material obtained in the case against Ms. Plavsic. A third motion of the 16th of January, access to the exculpatory statement of Sefer Halilovic; then the fourth is a motion of the 21st of January 2003 to compel production of exculpatory material. This I would call the second category, that is, the exculpatory material motions. And then the third category, containing only one motion, is the Prosecution motion of the 20th of February, 2003 for vacation of protective measures for a UN witness. Let me first start with the last one. Is the motion of the 20th of February, 2003 for vacation of protective measures for a UN witness, is it uncontested?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will soon give a decision on that. I then go back to the first category, that is the motion for an order suppressing illegally intercepted communications. The Chamber hopes that this motion can be decided at some time during next week, but it raises legal issues, factual issues that need proper attention, but we'll decide on that as soon as possible. The other motions are -- yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to the first motion, the motion to suppress the intercepted communications, I believe that there is not only questions of law in the motion but there also are questions of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I mentioned both, matters of law and fact, but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: With regard to that, Your Honour, would the Chamber envisage holding a hearing on the questions of fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you right now, but of course when preparing for this issue we will be confronted with perhaps facts that are not clear to the Chamber, but I first have to study further on it before I could give you an answer to your question. Then the last category, that's the category of four, the disclosure exculpatory -- the disclosure of exculpatory material. I have read the motions. I have also read what has been said about it during a recent meeting with Mr. Harhoff. I'd like to stress very much not to file motions when a telephone call could provide a solution to the problem. I might even stress that if no telephone call is made prior to filing a motion, the parties will be instructed, upon having received the motion, first to use the telephone before a decision will be given on the -- on the motion. I think whatever matter can be solved -- resolved by the parties should be resolved by the parties, and the Chamber would very much like to concentrate its energy on issues that are in dispute between the parties and remain to be in dispute between the parties. As far as a decision in this respect is concerned, I am aware that progress has been made in disclosure, and it might be not final, but I'd like to hear from the parties at this very moment whether the progress is such that it would be worth to see whether we can move on this way or whether there are specific issues which would ask for a decision, because the basis for the matter is clear, that there is a continuing obligation by the Prosecution to disclose whatever exculpatory material is known to it. Is there any observation needed in this respect at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President -- or Your Honour, we certainly agree with Your Honour's procedural requirements or suggestions as to the use of the telephone before using resources of the Prosecutor in the Tribunal to respond in writing, and so we accept that, and we encourage that, and we appreciate the decision and the guidance. In respect of each of those motions, we have continued to review the matters. In some cases we have turned over materials to the Defence. We are continuing to review each of the matters. I can't give you at this point in time a full representation as to whether those searches have been completed, but I can tell you they have been ongoing since we have received the motions, and we intend to abide by the requirements of Rule 68. That's all I have to report on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on what the Defence will say. When I referred to using the telephone, of course it might be clear to both parties that disclosure of exculpatory material is not dependent on a prior telephone call. That, of course, would be a distortion of the duty of the Prosecution, but if there's any specific issue that is raised in a motion, it could have been raised prior to that in a telephone, and that's what I refer to. Mr. Brashich, is there any comment you have on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence is mindful of the Court's position and of course will follow the suggestion. Until today, in the prior case in which I was involved in, and in this case, I thought I should strictly adhere to the rules, but I will follow the Court's suggestion, of course. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, to what rule are you referring? Is there any rule that says you should file a motion instead of using the telephone? I mean, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, there is no rule, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you said you would strict -- you were following --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Since there is no mention of telephones in the rules, I'm following the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's suggestion, and we will abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And we have since abided by it. Rather than using the telephone, which is sometimes difficult because of the time difference, we have directed two letters to the Prosecution with regard to additional Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: So we are following the senior legal officer's suggestion and will continue to do so. The only other comment that I would make, which again is exactly what Your Honour has said, that the obligation and the duty under Rule 68 is squarely on the Prosecution, and while we will remind the Prosecution from time to time that we have not been receiving what we consider Rule 68 material, I hope that we will be able to obviate the necessity of making motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brashich, I mentioned the matter because I saw in the transcript of the previous meeting with Mr. Harhoff that you expressed some concern that you would always have to call before getting disclosure of the exculpatory material. And of course it's clear between the parties that this is not the case. Then I'd like to move to our next subject. That is the submission of lists by -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Orie, but there are two additional motions that were not mentioned that were filed by the Prosecutor. I can just notify Your Honour what they are and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you give the dates as well, then I know how much I'm behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to. There is a motion -- and I have a copy of it here. There is a motion filed on the 10th of February, 2003, entitled Prosecution's Motion to Add Witness. And there is a motion of 14 November 2002, entitled Prosecution's Motion for Leave to Add Witness to List of Witnesses. Those are the two additional motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Neither one of those motions, Your Honour, were objected to or opposed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they are uncontested, and they give us a good link to our next subject, I would say, that is when the OTP -- when the Office of the Prosecutor will submit lists of witnesses. It has been delayed mainly due to the fact that, I think, the decision on the motion on adjudicated facts had not been delivered at that time. That decision has been delivered on the 28th of February, and I think that two weeks were granted to file the new list. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the obligation under the order of the Chamber was to provide the lists on Monday, the 15th. We have had a difficulty which resulted in my filing a motion for a request for a brief extension of time until the following Friday. I have set forth in my application the reasons for that request. I'm happy to explain them to Your Honour now, although they are in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see. You have received that application, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen it either, so that might cause a problem. If there are any copies available -- if you could just give a brief explanation, then we'll read it in full detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very brief motion. It was filed at about noon today. It is a motion that requests an extension of time because of staffing difficulties. The -- obviously, the analysis that is required under the Trial Chamber's order is something that we embarked upon immediately, but we are unable to complete because the lawyers, the senior lawyers who were involved in that analysis and the senior lawyers who will be involved in this trial, some are engaged in other commitments that have taken them away. One is out of the country conducting a case-related interview, and it is an interview that could not be rescheduled. So the ability to properly analyse and consult all of the issues that we are confronted with has been -- has been very slow and difficult. Another lawyer, a senior lawyer on the case, is involved in a sensitive interview as well that has been long scheduled. And so I find myself in a position with my colleagues who have to make these critical decisions, without a full team to do that, and I think it's important to make this final decision -- this analysis and set of decisions to have the full team present. There's the motion and the response by us is due on Monday, and we are requesting that we be granted four additional days when all of the people will once again be reassembled to make that critical analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Brashich, on the basis of the oral explanation, could you take a position or would you prefer, rather, to wait until --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I think I can take a position, Your Honour. What I'm unclear is what is the exact date that the Krajisnik Defence will get the list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that it would be the 19th. You're asking for the remainder of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be then the 19th of March, if I'm not making any mistake. No. It would be the 20th, I think. Yes, I have a calendar. I've been provided with calendar, and I think it would be the 20th --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but let me just see. Friday the 21st. I now know, Mr. Harmon, what confused me. You said you would have time until next Monday, the 15th, and next Monday is the 17th. So it would be the 21st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: The Krajisnik Defence is unhappy, but it understands that both sides have difficulties, and I'm sure that the Krajisnik Defence, during the course of this trial, will have the same difficulties and will have to ask the indulgence of both the Court and opposing counsel. So that is the position. I'm unhappy, but I'm going to have to live with it. The only other thing which I would like, Your Honour, with regard to this list, we have orders by the prior Trial Chamber of, I won't say preclusion, but orders limiting the scope of trial to that which had been filed with the final OTP pre-trial brief. What I would like to do, either make an oral motion or, if Your Honour wishes me to make a written submission, that the list of witnesses be deemed final and that only newly discovered witnesses have -- can leave be sought from the Trial Chamber to add to the list. I will be happy to make a motion in writing. I think the grounds for it are clear. We have been in ongoing discovery for now three years, and I think that this list should be final.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you have any -- but perhaps I would invite you to make a written submission to that extent. I gained the experience that what is -- what seems to be final or what should be final not always really is final, but I certainly do agree with you that such lists -- and therefore, I think it's good that the analysis by the Prosecution is taken seriously -- that such lists should not be subject to change every week, so they should at least have some finality in it and not just the start of an ongoing debate on who should be on the list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: In New York, we have a final adjournment or a final list, and then we a final final adjournment or list. Perhaps this should be a final final list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It sounds familiar: The last question, the very last question, the very very last question. Mr. Brashich, I think the message is clear. If you want to make any written submission in this respect, you're free to do so. Then -- so the parties can expect that the motion will be granted for time delay, for further delay for a couple of days, but it's not -- usually I take decisions only once I've seen the motions, so therefore I'll first look at it, but if it doesn't show anything else that I've heard until now, then the parties can expect the motion to be granted. The next issue on the list would be whether the Office of the Prosecutor has identified or wishes to identify any witnesses from whom a deposition could be taken in order to economise on the time spent in court. I would like to be informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was our intention when we submitted the list of final witnesses to include a column that would indicate whether or not we thought it was appropriate to depose a particular witness, so we agree in principle to the issue of depositions, and we will identify when we submit our list of final viva voce witnesses which of those witnesses we believe would be and could be deposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon. It will be clear to the Prosecution that it's a category in the 101 witnesses and not something additional to the 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. And, Your Honour, when you mention the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. categories of witnesses and the viva voce witnesses, I do have one question. I can reserve that question until the end of these proceedings, but it is a question relating to the numerical 101. I can raise it now if Your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless there's any objection, I would give you an opportunity to raise it now because we're now dealing with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- this is the issue: The Defence has filed a motion contesting the validity and the authentication of the intercepts. Obviously if there is an evidentiary hearing on that and the Court requires witnesses to be called, then we would call them in the evidentiary hearing, and we assume that those witnesses would not have to be recalled during the course of any trial and would not have to be added onto the list of 101 witnesses allowed for the Prosecution to present their case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they only have to testify on the issue of the intercept, then they should be examined as well, if needed, for the case, and they would not be counted as extra witnesses. Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. If we call these witnesses during an evidentiary hearing and the matters of legality of the intercept are decided, we see no reason why these witnesses have to be called once again to lay a foundation for the intercepts in the case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the issue. I'm not going to decide on it right now, but I'll have made a note of it. Then the next question, not the least important -- yes, if there's anything you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to state that we take no position at this particular time with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the next question to the Prosecution would be: What time do you expect the presentation of the case would take, if they can say something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Judge Orie, until we conclude our analysis of the list of viva voce witnesses, we are not in a position to give you an estimated length of the Prosecution's case. I think also there's an issue that needs to be at least discussed, and that is 92 bis. I could make a calculation on the estimate of the Prosecution's case, but the Defence has a right to cross-examine 92 bis, or they assert they have a right to cross-examine 92 bis witnesses, and how many of those 92 bis witnesses need to be cross-examined, I'm not sure. I can give you an estimate on the basis of no cross-examination and the evidence being accepted in toto, or -- and then I get into the area where I'm not able to give you any estimate whatsoever because I don't know how many of the 92 bis witnesses will be cross-examined. So the safest estimate I can give you is an estimate as to the estimated length of time on the viva voce witnesses, and I assume the presentation of the written evidence will be merely submitting the written document into evidence without anything further. Under those circumstances, that would take a minimal amount of time, but again if there is cross-examination, and I know in some case there have been sort of hybrid presentations of 92 bis evidence, that is an area where I'm unable to make a calculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And on the basis of viva voce witnesses, what would be your rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, that answer, Judge Orie, is something I can give you on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then, perhaps, wait until the 21st and not try to elicit any vague guesses of you which you might have to correct then anyhow. There's only one comment I'd like to make. You said that Defence is entitled to cross-examine 92 bis witnesses. I think it's subject to a decision of the Chamber under Rule 92 bis, under (E).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move to our next subject, and that would be the rules of the road. A number of questions have been put to me, questions contained in a memorandum of the 12th of February, 2003. These are just questions. Would there be any need to make observations on the questions, because -- is it enough for me to give you the views of the Chamber or would you like to comment on one or more of these items?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Depends on the Court's ruling, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- yes. If there's anything you'd like to bring to my attention before ruling, Mr. Brashich, you're free to do so. Observations after the ruling would easily result in a debate on the decision, and I'm not used to have lengthy debates of decisions taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've been following the jurisprudence and the holdings of other Chambers, and I have noted that one of the problems which I see is that during objections, much argument is had with the witness present. It would be the Krajisnik Defence position that should argument on an objection be allowed, then the witness should be excluded. And it's the only point that I would have to observe with regard to point number 1. With regard to point number 2, I would propose and the Krajisnik Defence's position would be that the ruling be made at the time of the objection. With regard to documents and proofs which have not yet been introduced into evidence, I think that is self-evident. You can't use documents, things, videotapes, if they have not been formally introduced into evidence and tested. That's at point 5, and 3 are more or less identical in concept. And the last thing, Your Honour: Again in reading transcripts of other trials or hearings before the various Chambers, the concept of an offer of proof is not covered by the rules, and we would like to have some guidance as to should the offer of proof be made orally or should it be done in writing? And of course if the offer of proof is made, how can it be best preserved for appeal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Harmon, is there any -- does the Prosecution have any views on what the answers should be to those questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in respect of the second item, the suggestion that the witness be excluded during the objection is one that I think depends on the nature of the objection. In respect of the use of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, are you referring to item 1 or item 2, because item 2 is objections will be ruled on immediately whenever possible; where there is presence of the witness seems to be covered by item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was referring to what Mr. Brashich had said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was about item 1, that I understand you well, may decide to bring the witness out of the courtroom when the objection is discussed. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I think that depends on the nature of the discussion of the objection. The use of documents and proofs not yet introduced into evidence, I think that documents have to be used and proofs proffered to be used before they are formally admitted into evidence. You have to be able to show the witness the items he's being examined about, and then thereafter you normally make an application for its admission. That is my comment in respect of item number 3. In respect of item number 9, the Prosecution's order of proof and advance notice of upcoming witnesses, the Prosecutor's office is willing to abide by whatever order this Chamber makes. Our request is that the equal order be applied to the Defence. So if we are required to turn over a name of a witness, for example, seven days in advance or ten days in advance, we would request that the Chamber make a similar order in identical terms when the Defence starts calling its witnesses. Those are the comments I have on the ten items that are before the Chamber in this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that it will be the circumstances of the objection that will guide the Trial Chamber whether to exclude the witness during argument. But as a general rule, it has been my experience that counsel should object and, just with one word, explain the objection; relevance, et cetera, et cetera. If anything goes further than that, then I would suggest that the Court should make a -- not a hard and fast rule, but more or less put counsel on notice that argument with the witness in the box should not be allowed. With regard to abiding by the same advance notice of witnesses, the Krajisnik Defence has no problem whatsoever. I had forgotten that there was a second page to my fax, so I turn it over and I find that there were three other points on that second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have four, 7 to 10 included.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes. Four, and one which I have already addressed. I really don't have any further comments other than those which I've noted. The only other thing which I would like to reply to Mr. Harmon is I was not envisaging showing the witness a document or a thing and then introducing it into evidence. What I was envisaging was having an opening statement in which audiovisual material or other material which is not in evidence is used during opening statements or is being discussed in the course of the trial before it has been properly introduced through a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood your number 10, exclusion of opinions -- no, no, no, it's not. Well, I understood you well. Then having heard -- I'll give you the provisional rulings on it. We have to deal with the matter. It has only been briefly introduced, briefly discussed, so I will give you the decisions. And if there would be any need, I hope there will not, to further refine any of these rulings, we'll hear from you and... The first thing about objections during the examination of witnesses. First of all, I'd like to stress that a flow of information not interrupted by objections is to be preferred. Many objections, especially in the common law traditions, serve to avoid that a jury hears something, sees something that it should not see or it should not hear. We are in a mixed system. That means that the Chamber is well aware of all the traps that might exist during the examination of a witness. I mean, a question that's leading, once it has been pronounced, of course might have influenced already a witness. If a question asks for hearsay, of course the Chamber will be aware that it does, if not yet from the question, then at least from the answer. So there would be less need to object since the -- since the functioning of the law of evidence is different in a bench trial compared to a jury trial. So the parties are invited to be very restrictive in objecting. When objections are made and are necessary, the Chamber would expect the parties to express these in one or just a couple of words, just as, "calls for speculation," or "relevance," or whatever. If there would be need for further argument, then that should, as a rule, be done in the absence of the witness. But I again repeat, I have the experience -- I had the experience recently that the witness was travelling in and out of the courtroom too much, and that, of course, undermines what the main purpose of what examining a witness is. That is, not to discuss procedural incidents, but it is to hear from the witness what he can answer to questions put to him. So if this may serve as a guidance to the parties. Be restrictive, be short, and if really necessary, we'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom so that any argument can be exchanged in respect of the objection raised. Second issue is objections will be ruled on immediately whenever possible. It might not always be possible, but whenever possible, a ruling will follow immediately. Then the display of proof that has not yet been introduced into evidence. There might be some confusion as to what exactly was asked, but as far as the opening statement is concerned, the parties are required to inform the other party about the material they intend to show, such as video material, during the opening statement. If there would be objections against the use of that material, that objection should be raised prior to the opening statements and, if necessary, there could be a hearing to suppress such material from the opening statement in order not to contaminate the opening statement. On the other hand, an opening statement is not an occasion at which you should object against the presentation of material. So it should be presented smoothly. But if there is any serious reason to object against the materials shown, it can be done previously. And therefore, it's necessary that the parties inform each other, disclose what material will be used during the opening statement. Then as far as the other evidence to be introduced is concerned, the Chamber intends to ask from the parties to exchange well in advance, and two weeks is in our mind, the exact sequence of calling these witnesses, the order of calling these witnesses, and at the same time indicate what exhibits will be used during the testimony of that witness. The Chamber will provide you with a format on how to exchange this information, and the Chamber would like to receive copies of this exchange of information by the parties. That would also enable the parties to think over well in advance to what exhibits objections should be raised. That can then be done if that exhibit is introduced. If there is no objection against a certain document or a certain object, the Chamber would prefer to deal with the admission into evidence at the end of the testimony of that witness. So that is we are not going to give a decision on the admission into evidence, but it is understood that if there is no objection, that at the very end of the testimony of that witness, perhaps even after he has left the courtroom, we'll ask the registry to guide us through the list of all documents that have been used during the testimony, and they will then all be admitted into evidence or not, but that's in order to not interrupt the testimony and again and again by decisions, this is admitted into evidence. This requires the parties to make clear what -- not to the Court mainly but especially to the other party what material it intends to use and introduce through that witness. The format of such lists will be provided to you by the senior legal officer, Mr. Harhoff. Standards of authentication was one of the questions. The Tribunal has not a specific standard of authentication. It's not required from the parties, but the introduction of each document to pay specific attention to the authentication. Authentication becomes an issue if the other party is objecting to the authenticity. And since you are aware two weeks in advance what documents presumably will be used or introduced through that witness, you always can raise the issue of authenticity, but you should give -- you should show good reasons to object against the authenticity of a document. So if a challenge is made, good reason should be shown immediately. Offers of proof. The question you asked mainly was whether it should be done in writing or orally. The answer is that it should be done in writing. I noticed that in your questions already, Mr. Brashich, and in your reference to what you might be used to, I find a lot of common law terminology. For example, "offer of proof" is, I think, something well known in the common law law of evidence but might not be that familiar to Judges that come from a civil law background. So this Chamber would very much appreciate if the parties would express themselves not primarily in the common law terminology which is linked very much to procedural systems but to briefly explain what it is about. It can be expected that the Trial Chamber, that the entire Trial Chamber, will have a civil law background. So there might be some need to avoid whatever malcommunication. The next question was what to do if lead counsel is unable to attend, if -- whether there would be any scheduling issues to allow the meeting of other obligations of trial counsel. Well, first of all, the Chamber expects that the trial counsel are dedicated full time to the case so that it would hardly happen, but of course one could imagine circumstances under which counsel would have to meet obligations elsewhere. Then co-counsel is expected to take over. And only in very, very exceptional circumstances the Chamber will consider to adjourn for the reason that both counsel have to meet obligations elsewhere. That will really be a rare exception. So the rule is co-counsel takes over. One question was about motions to strike unresponsive answers. I would say this is also an example very much of the -- outside the common law tradition, which might not be that necessary in a Bench trial where the Bench has heard it. So therefore, the Chamber considers such motions not to be needed. Number 9 of your list is the Prosecution's order of proof and advance notice of upcoming witnesses. I think I dealt with that. The same procedure applies to both parties. Then finally we have the exclusion of opinion statements from audiovisual material. I took it that you meant to say that whether -- if there's any audiovisual material and we can comment by a journalist - it's number 10 - that we would be confronted with comments or opinions of journalists or whomever or those persons interviewed. Is that what you are referring to or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent possible, the opinion should be not part of audiovisual material. On the other hand, if a journalist would say a few words on what happens which clarifies the issue, then of course there should be no specific problem. But here again, if the parties would exchange their lists of material that has already been disclosed two weeks in advance, you could always check in the transcripts of the audiovisual material whether there is any reason, for example, to look at this material without sound, which sometimes solves the problem. But there again, I expect the parties to review the material in advance and to come up with objections as to listening also to opinions contained in that material prior to it being shown to a witness, especially if this could influence the witness, and a decision would then be taken on what exactly would appear as opinion in such material. This is as far as the rules of the road is concerned, what I'd like to tell you, and I think it covers most if not all of your questions, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next point on the agenda is -- was a question mark, trial management seminar. If the Defence would be interested, the Chamber will offer a seminar to introduce the Defence to especially the services of the Tribunal. For example, to yet acquainted with some of the registry, people from security, people from OLAD, so that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they can explain how they work so you can be better aware of what to expect and what not to expect from those officers of the Tribunal. An explanation on the court reporting, perhaps training in the use of the LiveNote programme which appears on your laptop. And I can tell you, I could not do without this LiveNote programme. So therefore, if the Defence is interested to have such a -- such a trial management seminar, I'd rather say meet the people of the Tribunal and see what they are doing and get acquainted with that, it's an offer, it's a standing offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Any help is appreciated by the Krajisnik Defence, and I would appreciate being given such a seminar for my Defence team. It can only help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask that such a seminar will be prepared. I take it that the Office of the Prosecution -- I know there is equality of arms, but they might be acquainted already with the services of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The next issue would be, and that, Mr. Krajisnik, would be more directly related to you, because until now we have -- you may -- you may be seated. You don't have to stand always if I address you. Until now, we have dealt with all kind of procedural issues, and one would easily forget that a trial is not just a matter of procedural technicalities but is about a person who stands trial in this Tribunal. So therefore, I'd like now to focus my attention on you personally and would like to know whether there's anything in respect of your conditions of detention, your health, or whatever you would like to bring to my attention at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to thank you for providing me with this opportunity, Mr. President, to address you. I'll be very brief, with your permission, but there are a few things that I would like to -- a few issues I would like to raise that might help you, this Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, but above all, myself. First of all, I would like to ask you and the Prosecution -- well, there are two issues that concern, that are related to the Prosecution. One of the issues concerns witnesses who are in the field and who are visited by our investigators. They are under psychological pressure. They think that they might be accused by the Prosecutors, and they're very reluctant to provide our Defence - my Defence - statements. And for this reason I would like to ask the Prosecution whether they could make a statement stating that witnesses have the right and perhaps even the moral duty, if not the legal obligation, to provide the Defence with statements as well as the Prosecution. One example, Your Honour: If a witness had been visited and said that witnesses [as interpreted] came to see him, that he was ordered that he shouldn't give anyone else a statement and that he was protected by the Prosecution, I have his name and I have the statement of our investigator. And the second thing that concerns the Prosecution, I think that the porte-parole of the Prosecution quite by mistake, a few days ago, watched the Belgrade television and said that my Defence requested that the hearing should be postponed on three occasions because this had to do with the length of my detention. The second thing I want to ask you about is that I submitted a request to the Trial Chamber that was -- preceded you, and it had to do with the privileged telephone link that each accused has, a telephone link to co-counsel and to lead counsel. I have no objections to make, no criticisms of my counsel to make, but they are in America, and when I am asleep -- when they are asleep, I'm free. And when they are working, naturally it's night over here. So I have few possibilities to contact my lawyer in America. It's easier for me to contact co-counsel. And after three years, I don't know which address this concerns, I was permitted to speak to co-counsel, to contact my co-counsel. But today, I have been informed that this decision has been revoked. It is very important for me to be able to speak to people who are in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Serbia and in Republika Srpska. It's important for me to be able to give them suggestions about this problem so as to be able to prepare my defence as best as possible. What I would also like to add is -- well, the lawyer's here, but very often documents which are sent by fax, by some mistake they don't get to me, they don't reach me, and they're very important. And in that regard, I would like to thank you. In a certain sense, I am more assured that the proceedings will commence, because I can see a permanent Presiding Judge, because up until now we have only had a provisional Trial Chamber. And finally, Your Honour, I'm an innocent man. I'm not guilty, and this Trial Chamber will establish that this is the case and I'm just asking you to help me have a good and fair defence and to help me prove relevant facts. I would like to ask you, Mr. President. You talked about intercepted conversations today. That's called phone tapping, illegal phone tapping in my country, and I'm telling you, this is completely illegal, which is why I'm asking you to organise an investigation and to bring the persons concerned to show that this was illegally carried out. They were listening in to the president of the parliament, the Prime Minister of the parliament before the crisis commenced. I thank you very much, and I hope that this process, these proceedings will be fair and that I will go away from here as a free man. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The observations you made were mainly in respect of the proceedings rather than your personal situation. Is there anything else you would like to add in respect of your health situation or whatever of a personal nature rather than related to the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I took advantage of this opportunity since I am a former politician. There are items that concern my health and other items too, so I suggested certain items. As far as my health is concerned, I'm healthy now and I can only say the best about Mr. McFadden and his employees. I have no objections to make at all. This is why I'm asking you to help me with regard to these other issues that are of importance to me. Perhaps even more important than my health. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Don't underestimate the importance of your health, Mr. Krajisnik, but I will briefly respond to some of your concerns. First of all about the witnesses, the witnesses that should be free to come and testify before this Court. If there would be any witness that would be afraid of being accused by the Prosecution -- being accused is one thing, but even being prosecuted, that would even be another thing -- there are technical rules in respect of applications for safe conduct for witnesses. So if necessary, Defence counsel will know how to apply for that. You raised another issue. I would not like to respond to that immediately, but that seems to relate to a matter which I heard some British and some American lawyers debating about for quite some time: Is there any property in a witness once a witness has been approached by one of the parties, to what extent the other party should stay away from that witness. I don't know whether you refer to that when you say protected or stay away, but if the parties would not agree on what would be allowed in this respect, I'd like to be informed so that we -- that I at least would know that the parties have a different view on the matter. So therefore, the parties are invited to discuss the matter among themselves and inform the Chamber if there's any disagreement in this respect. Then the second issue you raised is about communication with counsel. Communication with counsel, privileged - that means confidential - should be possible in order to enable you to prepare for your defence. I'm not saying whether at all times of the day you would have a privileged telephone always available, but as a basic rule, such communication, whether it's in written form or it is by telephone, should be made available to you. You also gave your view on the illegality of the interception of communication that the Prosecution intends to present as evidence. A motion is pending on the issue, and proper attention will be paid to that. Finally, you asked these proceedings to be fair. The Trial Chamber will guarantee the fairness of these proceedings. That is the task of the Trial Chamber under the Statute of this Tribunal, and the Trial Chamber takes this task very seriously. Is there any other issue to be raised at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is nothing on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to demonstrate to you how seriously these matters we take, the registrar informs me that she already tried to contact colleagues on a decision on privileged telephone conversation with co-counsel, but she has not yet received an answer, but this just demonstrates how seriously these matters are taken. You have no further matters to be raised, Mr. Brashich?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then finally, although it's not very usual that a Judge expresses himself on what happens in the world, I would like to inform you that I was shocked by what happened today to Mr. Djindjic. If there are no further matters to be discussed, we'll adjourn, presumably until the next extra Pre-Trial Conference, but the parties will be informed about that.
